title: Que horas são? — time, days and routines
goal: Tell the time, name the days and describe your daily routine — while meeting Portugal's way of naming the days, which no other major European language uses.
bekal: answer *Que horas são?* correctly, including the exception *É uma hora*
name the days of the week and the parts of the day
use the time prepositions: *às nove*, *de manhã*, *ao sábado*

dialogs.title: Diálogo — Na cozinha, de manhã
dialogs.intro: Seven in the morning. Budi walks into the kitchen and finds Dona Fernanda has already made coffee.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: Good morning. What time is it?

lines.speaker: D. Fernanda:
lines.text: São sete e um quarto. Hoje tens aulas?
lines.id: It's a quarter past seven. Do you have classes today?
lines.literal: are seven and a quarter. today you-have classes?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Tenho. As aulas são de segunda a sexta, das nove ao meio-dia.
lines.id: I do. Classes are Monday to Friday, from nine till noon.
lines.literal: I-have. the(pl) classes are from second to sixth, from-the(pl) nine to-the mid-day.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: À tarde estudo em casa. Às vezes vou ao museu.
lines.id: In the afternoon I study at home. Sometimes I go to the museum.
lines.literal: at-the afternoon I-study in home. at-the(pl) times I-go to-the museum.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Ao sábado durmo até tarde. Ao domingo almoço fora.
lines.id: On Saturdays I sleep in. On Sundays I have lunch out.
lines.literal: at-the Saturday I-sleep until late. at-the Sunday I-lunch outside.

lines.speaker: D. Fernanda:
lines.text: Aqui o almoço é sempre à uma e jantamos às oito.
lines.id: Here lunch is always at one and we have dinner at eight.
lines.literal: here the lunch is always at-the one and we-dine at-the(pl) eight.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Em Portugal janta-se tarde, não é?
lines.id: In Portugal people eat dinner late, don't they?
lines.literal: in Portugal dines-oneself late, not is?

lines.speaker: D. Fernanda:
lines.text: Tarde? Em Espanha jantam às dez!
lines.id: Late? In Spain they have dinner at ten!
lines.literal: late? in Spain they-dine at-the(pl) ten!

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Pois é. Então às oito ainda é cedo!
lines.id: True. So eight o'clock is still early!
lines.literal: indeed is. so at-the(pl) eight still is early!

notes: **São sete, but É uma.** Time takes *ser*, and the form follows the number: plural for two and up (*são duas*, *são sete*), singular for one (*é uma hora*). Notice also that the number is **feminine** — *são duas*, not *são dois* — because *horas* is feminine.

**Portuguese days are numbered.** *Segunda-feira* means "second day", *terça* third, up to *sexta*, sixth. Only Saturday and Sunday have names of their own. This system comes from the 6th-century church calendar, and Portuguese is the **only major European language** that still uses it.

**Ao sábado means "on Saturdays", not "on Saturday".** For repeated habits, Portugal uses *ao sábado*, *ao domingo*, *à segunda*; Brazil uses the plural *aos sábados*. For one particular upcoming day, use *no sábado*: *no sábado vou a Sintra* (this Saturday).

**Janta-se tarde** is a subjectless construction, like English "people eat late" or "dinner is eaten late". The *se* here doesn't mean "oneself" — it signals that no one in particular is doing the action. It's very common on signs: *vende-se* (for sale), *aluga-se* (for rent), *fala-se inglês* (English spoken).

**Durmo, not dormo.** A group of *-ir* verbs change their vowel in the *eu* form only: *dormir* → *durmo*, *subir* → *subo*, *preferir* → *prefiro*, *servir* → *sirvo*. The other forms stay regular: *dormes*, *dorme*, *dormimos*, *dormem*. The change keeps the word easy to say, and you only need to remember it for *eu*.

grammars.title: Telling the time
body: Minutes are added with *e* and subtracted with *menos*. After half past, the Portuguese usually count down to the next hour.
after: **To ask the time:** *Que horas são?* To ask what time something happens: *A que horas...?* — and the answer always uses *às*: *às nove*, *às três e meia*. The one exception: *à uma* (singular).
The part of the day is added with *de* or *da*: *às oito **da** manhã* (8 am), *às três **da** tarde* (3 pm), *às dez **da** noite* (10 pm). When there's no doubt, it can be left out.
On train and airport timetables and at the movies, the Portuguese use the 24-hour clock and read it straight: *o comboio parte às dezoito e trinta* (18:30, i.e. 6:30 pm).

grammars.title: Days and parts of the day
body: All the day names are **masculine** except those ending in *-feira*, which are feminine.
after: In conversation, the word *feira* is almost always dropped: *Vejo-te na quinta* = "see you Thursday". Write it in full, say it short.

English names its days after gods and planets — Saturn's day, the Sun's day. Portuguese kept only two real names: *sábado* comes from the Hebrew *Sabbath*, and *domingo* from Latin *dies Dominicus*, "the Lord's day".

grammars.title: Time prepositions
body: Four prepositions handle almost every time expression at A1.
after: **De manhã but à tarde and à noite.** There's no reason; it's just a habit to memorize. The three are often said in a row, so practice them as one sequence: *de manhã, à tarde, à noite*.
*Há* also means "for" or "ago": *estou em Portugal há dois meses* = "I've been in Portugal for two months". Notice that the verb stays in the present, unlike English "I've been".

blocks.text: **Breakfast in Portugal is *o pequeno-almoço*** — literally "little lunch". In Brazil it's *o café da manhã*. This is one of the most visible differences on hotel menus, and one that often confuses learners who study from both Portuguese and Brazilian sources at once.

exercises.prompt: Write out the time in Portuguese.
Fill in the right time preposition.
items: ____ sábado que vem vou a Sintra.
Sometimes I go to the museum.

exercises.prompt: Spaced review — unit 7. Translate into Portuguese without looking back at the unit.
items: The pharmacy is next to the bank.
The key is on the table.

answers: É uma hora. — São três e meia. — São sete e um quarto. — São dez menos um quarto. — É meio-dia. — São dez e dez da noite.
às — de — à — Ao — No — à
Que horas são? — São oito e meia. — As aulas são de segunda a sexta. — Ao sábado durmo até tarde. — Jantamos às oito. — Às vezes vou ao museu.
Onde fica a estação? — A farmácia fica ao lado do banco. — Vire à esquerda. — É longe daqui? — A chave está em cima da mesa.
